papers.title: Reply to: Structural polymorphism of amyloid fibrils in ATTR amyloidosis revealed by cryo-electron microscopy
papers.abstract: In the paper by Nguyen et al, published in Nature Communications in 2024, we describe structural polymorphism in fibrils extracted from patients with ATTR amyloidosis. ATTR amyloidosis is characterized by deposition of transthyretin amyloid fibrils across multiple organs, resulting in marked phenotypic variability. Previous studies on ATTR suggest its phenotypic variability may be linked to differences in fibril structure, as demonstrated in amyloid diseases such as AA amyloidosis, tauopathies, or synucleinopathies. Thus far, most ATTR fibrils adopt a strikingly similar fold across patients and affected organs. The most notable exception is described in the study by Nguyen et al., where we report the identification of two co-existing polymorphs in cardiac fibrils from three patients with the ATTRv-I84S variant. These cardiac polymorphs differ in conformation of the segment Gly57 to Gly67, termed the gate, which regulates access to a central polar channel within the fibril core. In one polymorph, the gate adopts an open conformation, exposing the channel, whereas in the other it is closed, shielding it. Whether these polymorphs extend beyond cardiac tissue remains unknown. Here, we address this question by extending our analysis to additional organs from a fourth patient with ATTRv-I84S amyloidosis.

papers.title: CryoSHIELDs: tunable amphipathic peptide additives for cryo-EM
papers.abstract: While cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) has transformed structural biology, sample preparation remains a major determinant of success. Specifically, the air-water interface (AWI) can damage complexes, impose preferred orientation, and reduce particle density. Here, we introduce cryoSHIELDs, a chemically diverse library of peptide additives designed to passivate the AWI and improve cryo-EM grid preparation. Across 24 protein systems spanning GPCRs, ABC and SLC transporters, soluble and Fab-containing complexes, and enzymes, cryoSHIELDs increased the success rate of structure determination. Individual cryoSHIELDs improved particle density, angular sampling, complex stability, and, for routine targets, map quality and resolution. This toolkit enabled the structural characterization of important targets, including the ABCC6 transporter, revealing unique TMD0-mediated stabilization, and DAMGO-bound -opioid receptor-Gi complex using substantially lower protein concentration. CryoSHIELDs provide a simple, tunable, and broadly applicable platform for more reliable cryo-EM in discovery biology and structure-based drug development.

papers.title: Direct detection of electrogenic polyamine transport
papers.abstract: Polyamines are cationic metabolites that support critical cellular processes including transcription, translation, and cell proliferation. Although polyamine synthesis and transport are emerging therapeutic targets in human disease, the polyamine transport system remains poorly understood. ATP13A2-4 were recently identified as endolysosomal polyamine exporters, transporting putrescine (PUT), spermidine (SPD), and spermine (SPM) from the vesicular lumen to the cytosol. Despite interest in pharmacologically targeting these transporters, existing assays of transporter function rely on indirect or endpoint measures that cannot resolve transport as it occurs. Here, we report the first voltage-clamp recordings of polyamine transporter activity, directly detecting ATP13A2- and ATP13A3-mediated charge movement across cell membranes. When expressed in Xenopus oocytes, these transporters localized to the plasma membrane, enabling electrophysiological measurements. Polyamines induced inward currents dependent on transporter catalytic activity, and their dose-dependence correlated with ATPase assays. ATP13A2 currents were largest in response to SPM, whereas ATP13A3 currents were largest with PUT, consistent with their established substrate preferences. Polyamine-induced currents were blocked by the polyamine transport inhibitor AMXT-1501. These findings establish ATP13A2 and ATP13A3 as electrogenic polyamine pumps and demonstrate the utility of two-electrode voltage clamp as a label-free, transporter-resolved assay to complement other approaches in polyamine transporter-targeted drug discovery.

papers.title: Mechanical fidelity of brain tissue phantoms: A comparative experimental characterization of equilibrium and dissipative behavior
papers.abstract: Despite lacking a dedicated structural function, brain tissue is exposed to severe mechanical loading during accidents and trauma, with potentially permanent or lethal consequences. Therefore, characterizing its mechanical behavior assumes particular importance for designing protective equipment, planning surgeries, and training neurosurgeons, tasks that often rely on physical brain replicas made from phantom materials. Although the mechanics of brain tissue has been extensively studied, the selection of suitable phantom materials still relies on simplified metrics that fail to capture the highly nonlinear and rate-dependent behavior of the brain. In this work, we characterize the mechanical response at low-to-medium strain rates of common synthetic brain phantom materials, including Sylgard 527, Ecoflex Gel, and a composite hydrogel, and establish rigorous comparisons with porcine brain tissue as a benchmark. To this end, we employ a multi-step stress relaxation protocol under both uniaxial extension and compression across two different strain rates, introduce thermodynamic metrics, and perform comparisons based on rigorous statistical analysis. In particular, we isolate the thermodynamic equilibrium stress-strain curves, representing the baseline material's response, from rate-dependent dissipative inelastic effects, relatable to viscoelastic and poroelastic mechanisms. Our results provide a thorough comparison, revealing critical limitations in existing simulant materials and highlighting significant space for developing improved brain surrogates. The comprehensive dataset collected can also support the calibration of constitutive models, enhancing the predictive accuracy of numerical simulations involving brain tissue and its surrogates. More broadly, this study highlights the need to move beyond simplistic, scalar-metric-based comparisons of mechanical responses across materials.

papers.title: CopY as a Transcriptional Duet Orchestrating Copper Homeostasis via Asymmetry-Dependent DNA Affinity
papers.abstract: Copper is essential yet potentially toxic, requiring tight regulation of intracellular concentration. The copper-responsive transcriptional repressor CopY is unusual among bacterial metalloregulators because it occupies two operator sites within the cop promoter. Although two CopY dimers bind these operators independently, the mechanistic significance of this dual-operator architecture remains unclear. Here, we combine biochemical assays, circular dichroism (CD), and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) distance measurements to define the molecular basis of CopY-mediated repression. CopY binds the proximal operator with higher affinity than the distal operator. CD measurements further show that DNA binding increases CopY thermal stability, with greater stabilization by the proximal operator. Conversely, DNA-based EPR measurements reveal comparable CopY-induced compaction of both operators. Thus, protein stabilization and DNA deformation represent distinct components of repression. Moreover, site-directed spin labeling and EPR demonstrate that the metal binding domain is conformationally heterogeneous and highly flexible. DNA binding has only a marginal effect on this flexibility. Thus, the metal site is not a rigid pocket but a dynamic one, even in the DNA-bound repressor, a property that may facilitate Cu(I) capture and hence derepression once copper levels rise. We propose that the proximal operator serves as a high-affinity anchoring site, whereas the distal operator primarily promotes promoter remodeling, and that the plasticity of the metal binding domain is retained in the DNA-bound repressor. Together, these findings support a "transcriptional duet" model in which two CopY dimers bound to non-equivalent operators make distinct and complementary contributions to repression.

papers.title: Macroscopic Vibronic Coherence and Non-Dispersive Soliton Propagation Across a Protein-Solvent Interface
papers.abstract: A foundational tenet of modern biophysics dictates that protein-solvent interactions and charge-transport dynamics operate strictly within microscopic, sub-nanometer boundaries where long-range coordination is natively suppressed by rapid room-temperature thermal dephasing. Here, we report an unexpected phenomenon that fundamentally challenges this paradigm: the long-distance, quantum-coherent communication between isolated protein samples in aqueous solution across macroscopic spatial separations. By mapping the distance-dependence of a weak, protein-emitted electromagnetic field on the response dynamics of an adjacent complex, we demonstrate that this inter-protein communication establishes a stable, intermolecular vibronic coupling operating across millimeter-scale distances up to at least 40 mm. This field interference induces a robust quantum coherence that lowers the local potential energy surface, transforming the coupled protein-solvent network into an un-attenuated, low-barrier energy transfer conduit. This stabilized pathway launches a topologically protected, non-dispersive soliton that exhibits exceptional phase stability against room-temperature thermal dephasing. These findings provide definitive empirical evidence of a sophisticated, field-driven quantum infrastructure embedded within a biological macromolecule. More explicitly, they reveal that a protein can possess an inherent capacity to preserve coherent wave propagation over macroscopic scales previously deemed impossible in room-temperature aqueous environments.

papers.title: Activation pathway of the human voltage-gated proton channel
papers.abstract: Many protein functions are coupled to proton transfer, yet the underlying mechanisms remain extremely difficult to resolve by experiment or conventional molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. The human voltage-gated proton channel HV1 (hHV1) plays key roles in human physiology, but how voltage and pH together drive its activation remains unresolved. Experimental structures of hHV1 are limited to the X-ray structure of a mouse chimera and NMR models of a truncated hHV1, both representing an intermediate resting state. Here we determine the activation pathway of hHV1, together with structural models of its resting and activated states, using an approach that integrates all-atom continuous constant-pH MD (CpHMD), weighted-ensemble (WE) path sampling, and AlphaFold modeling. Starting from an AlphaFold model selected for consistency with resting-state experimental data, over 100 s of simulations reveal a mechanism in which transmembrane voltage, assisted by proton titration, drives an outward displacement of the transmembrane segment S4 accompanied by a one-click reorganization of countercharge pairings. These events are enabled by a delicately balanced electrostatic landscape and pH-modulated breathing motions in the resting state that prime the channel for protonation-state switches upon voltage sensing, a principle that may underlie other proton-coupled voltage-gating processes. The simulations also uncover lipid-binding sites at which POPG selectively stabilizes the S4-up conformation, whereas POPE can stabilize either state. These predictions are validated against extensive electrophysiology, mutagenesis data, and new smFRET experiments, which support the one-click S4 displacement and the lipid effects. WE-CpHMD, implemented in the AMBER package, is applicable to other proton-coupled processes that remain elusive.

papers.title: Multi-modal ion-transport function of potassium channelrhodopsins
papers.abstract: Light-gated K+ channelrhodopsins (KCRs) are recognized as an ideal neuronal silencing tool in optogenetics. KCRs contain functionally important residues for a light-driven H+ pump bacteriorhodopsin, but their roles have been unclear. Utilizing electrophysiological methods, we demonstrate that KCRs function as a light-driven H+ pump in the absence of K+. Transport experiments using pH electrodes further elucidated the function of the H+-pump, which operates even in the presence of K+. The hypothesis that the H+ pump exerts a blocking effect on K+ transport in KCRs has been postulated. Furthermore, we ascertained that there was conversion of KCRs from the H+ pump into the H+ channel by light, yet this conversion was never reversed. However, the addition of K+ resulted in the formation of the K+ channel. KCRs exhibit three distinct functional states, H+ pump, H+ channel, and K+ channel. These multifaceted functions are modulated by environmental ions and light.

papers.title: The biophysical interaction network that couples zona occludens-1 to membrane proteins at tight junctions
papers.abstract: Tight junctions are dynamic membrane-bound protein assemblies that maintain barrier function for tissues as cells divide, grow, and move through development and throughout life. Maintenance of tissue barriers requires spatially separated intracellular and extracellular signaling pathways to be linked through novel and dynamic protein interaction networks. Tight junction intracellular signaling is governed by zona occludens-1 (ZO-1), a Membrane-Associated GUanylate Kinase (MAGUK) family protein that recruits and assembles transmembrane proteins and scaffolds them to the actin cytoskeleton through its own oligomerization, localization to membranes, and phase separation. Here we report comprehensive quantitative studies that nearly completely maps the intracellular interaction network between ZO-1 and tight junction transmembrane proteins that elucidates the biophysical principles governing their binding and a mechanism for how stimuli transmit through membranes. We establish where, how, and with whom each protein interacts, and identify how membrane proteins enable ZO-1 and greater tight junction function through specific interactions or by phase separation. Our findings reveal the intracellular interactome that triggers and regulates tight junction assembly, the active and direct roles each membrane protein plays in these processes, and provide a mechanism for how intra/extracellular signaling is coupled to transmit mechanochemical signals between cells via tight junctions. These insights provide a prospective blueprint for how other MAGUK/membrane protein interaction networks form and function across biology.

papers.title: Asymmetric assembly underlies activation mechanism of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels
papers.abstract: G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK; Kir3) channels are principal effectors of inhibitory GPCR signaling. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule imaging, electrophysiology and molecular dynamics to define the architecture and activation of neuronal GIRK1/2 channels. GIRK1/2 preferentially assembles as an asymmetric heterotetramer containing one GIRK1 and three GIRK2 subunits. Three PIP2; molecules bound to GIRK2 promote partial cytoplasmic-domain docking, whereas engagement of a fourth PIP2 by GIRK1 completes docking and opens the helix bundle crossing gate. GIRK1 also remodels the electrostatic environment beneath the selectivity filter, where its E141 and D173 residues create a permeation module that enhances K+ conduction. The GIRK1-selective activator ML297 binds at the GIRK1-GIRK2 interface and controls both permeation and gating. These findings establish how asymmetric assembly couples sequential lipid-dependent gating to efficient K+ permeation and GIRK1-dependent pharmacological activation.

papers.title: Chameleonicity Beyond Compactness: Conformational Persistence and Passive Permeability Across 20 PROTAC Ensembles
papers.abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) are large, flexible molecules that frequently extend beyond conventional drug-like chemical space, including Lipinski's rule-of-five boundaries. Their membrane permeability has often been linked to molecular chameleonicity and the ability to adopt compact conformations with reduced polar surface exposure; however, the underlying conformational determinants remain unclear. Here, we investigated 20 PROTACs spanning distinct passive-permeability classes using enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics (ES-MD). All permeability classes accessed compact states with low radius of gyration (Rg) and polar surface area (PSA), indicating that compact-state accessibility alone does not distinguish permeable from non-permeable PROTACs. We therefore introduce maximum ring size (MRS), defined as the size of the largest intramolecular hydrogen-bonded ring, as a metric for identifying compact conformations stabilized by long-range intramolecular hydrogen bonding. Like the other descriptors examined, MRS neither separates nor ranks the permeability classes, but helps locate folded states in the large ensemble. Representative compact conformations from selected highly permeable, moderately permeable, and non-permeable compounds were subsequently examined by all-atom unbiased MD in water and chloroform. The highly permeable PROTAC held a closed-flat ensemble in both environments, but in two structurally distinct arrangements, whereas the other two redistributed across heterogeneous ensembles. Passive diffusion therefore appears to depend on the population, stability, and environment-dependent persistence of permeable-like states rather than on compactness alone.

papers.title: Unraveling phenotypic variation in multiscale behavioral dynamics
papers.abstract: Behavioral variability reflects differences in internal and external parameters and provides a substrate for natural selection. However, uncovering its structure is challenging because behavior evolves nonlinearly across multiple timescales. Our goal is to reconstruct phenotypic variation from finite behavioral observations without prescribing the scales at which individuals should be compared. To achieve this, we introduce a multiscale dissimilarity that compares dynamics across all statistically resolvable resolutions by constructing reduced transfer operators at progressively finer scales and weighting their differences by finite-sampling uncertainty. This dissimilarity defines a geometry of dynamical phenotypes, which we reconstruct using diffusion maps. We show that the resulting phenotypic coordinates locally follow the parameter directions to which dynamics are most sensitive. We validate our approach in a stochastic model and apply it to bacterial and larval zebrafish behavior. In bacteria, we identify run speed as a major component of inter-individual variability, associated with the chemotaxis protein CheB. In zebrafish, we find that prior prey experience reshapes behavioral dynamics and phenotypic variability, with paramecia experience concentrating fish in a prey-capture-associated region of phenotypic space. Together, these results provide a framework for identifying internal and environmental variables that structure dynamical phenotypes across scales.

papers.title: Lipid Defect Analyzer (LipiDeA): A Python Framework for Quantifying Lipid Packing Defects in Curved and Neutral Lipid-Containing Membranes
papers.abstract: Lipid packing defects expose hydrophobic regions of membranes and influence protein-membrane recognition, membrane remodeling, and lipid sensing. Quantitative analysis of these defects remains challenging for heterogeneous membranes with strong curvature, mixed bilayer and monolayer organization, and substantial neutral-lipid content. Here, we present Lipid Defect Analyzer (LipiDeA), an open-source Python framework for quantitative analysis of lipid packing defects in complex membrane systems. LipiDeA reconstructs membrane surfaces using triangulated meshes that adapt to local membrane geometry and identifies packing defects from lipid coverage of the reconstructed surface. The framework further classifies bilayer and monolayer regions, resolves defect properties according to local membrane curvature, and distinguishes defects associated with phospholipid tails and neutral lipids. Validation using planar and buckled DPPC bilayers reproduced previously reported packing defect constants and showed that defects preferentially occur in positively curved membrane regions. Application to lipid-droplet-like membranes revealed composition- and topology-dependent defect formation, with the largest defects occurring during the transition from bilayer-dominated to monolayer-containing membranes and distinct defect properties for DAG- and TAG-containing systems. These results highlight the importance of local membrane geometry and composition in determining lipid packing defects.

papers.title: Joint protein, mRNA and DNA sequence design and optimization with nucleotide-level Potts models
papers.abstract: Protein design typically generates amino acid sequences first and then translates them into DNA post-hoc limiting control over the nucleotide sequence via codon choice at design time. We introduce NuCaliby, a structure-conditioned model that jointly designs amino acid, mRNA, and DNA sequences of a protein at nucleotide resolution. NuCaliby predicts a Potts model over a nucleotide graph, trained using amino acid supervision by marginalizing over synonymous codons. It preserves residue-level designability on par with the original Caliby model. Its energy-based formulation supports composable inference-time guidance from sequence-level objectives through proposal construction and candidate acceptance, allowing the incorporation of biological proxies into the coding nucleotide sequence. Under organism-specific tRNA adaptation guidance, NuCaliby improves adaptation to host tRNA pools beyond synonymous sequence space, trading-off self-consistency. NuCaliby also embeds specified RNA motif sequences directly into coding sequences, avoiding the combinatorial growth required for the same task at the amino-acid level. In wet lab experiments, NuCaliby produces expressible and soluble proteins on par with state of the art methods, while enabling more complex nucleotide-level control and optimization. Together, these results extend protein design beyond the amino acid level, enabling joint optimization across the central dogma of molecular biology. The code and model weights are available here: https://github.com/blazejba/NuCaliby

papers.title: Bilayer-bound structure of SARS-CoV-2 Envelope protein in complex with a host PDZ domain
papers.abstract: Small multifunctional viral membrane proteins called viroporins are attractive drug targets but are difficult to structurally characterize in a lipid-bilayer environment. We have successfully reconstituted the full-length Envelope (E) protein from SARS-CoV-2 in a lipid-bilayer, co-assembled with a native host factor that binds to E, the PDZ domain 2 of ZO1. We have leveraged the enhancement afforded by dynamic nuclear polarization NMR to determine that the ensemble-averaged oligomer state of E is a pentamer. Complexing the protein with a host PDZ domain did not impact the oligomer state, but resulted in structuring of the last four residues of E, and immobilization of the PDZ domain near the lipid surface. Combined with secondary structure information derived from the chemical shifts, these data were used to model an E protein pentamer together with the PDZ protein dimer. Inclusion of a relevant host factor, as well as a complex lipid bilayer that mimics conditions in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, approaches native conditions, and addresses the ongoing controversy regarding the functional oligomer state in an infected cell.

papers.title: Substrate accessibility of bovine milk proteins to a Pseudomonas metalloprotease reveals why caseins are more readily hydrolysed than whey proteins
papers.abstract: Structure-aware proteolysis prediction often ranks candidate cleavage sites using solvent accessibility from static protein structures, yet this assumption is rarely tested against native-state cleavage data. We examined this problem using AprX, a serralysin-family protease that readily hydrolyses caseins but shows lower activity toward native whey proteins. Across six bovine milk proteins, sequence compatibility and local scissile-bond accessibility did not separate caseins from whey proteins. In contrast, accessibility fell progressively in whey proteins as the required contiguous substrate window increased, reaching 0% across the working P4-P4' footprint, while all evaluable casein windows remained accessible in isolated-chain ensembles. Local remodelling showed that whey segments could still adopt AprX-compatible backbone geometry. An external thermolysin benchmark rejected a rigid whole-protein clash metric, but did not alter the contiguous-accessibility result. These findings identify footprint-scale accessibility as a distinct structural variable and show why single-residue solvent exposure can overestimate protease accessibility in folded proteins.

papers.title: Activation thresholds set the speed of biochemical trigger waves
papers.abstract: Trigger waves are positive feedback-mediated traveling waves that propagate without slowing down or diminishing in amplitude, enabling biochemical coordination over distances where diffusion alone would be insufficient. Apoptosis can spread as trigger waves of caspase activity, as demonstrated in Xenopus eggs and egg extracts. We measured apoptotic wave speeds in extracts at two cell cycle states and found that waves propagated more slowly in M-phase arrested cytostatic factor (CSF) extracts than in interphase extracts (21 versus 27 m min-1). Luther's equation, v=2{surd}D{kappa}, predicts wave speed from the diffusion coefficient D and the positive-feedback doubling rate {kappa}. However, D and {kappa} were comparable between the two extracts and could not explain the speed difference. This discrepancy highlighted a key limitation of the classical equation: it does not account for an activation threshold in trigger wave initiation, and in fact the threshold required to trigger apoptosis was found to differ between cell cycle states. We therefore extended Luther's equation to include such a threshold, obtaining v{propto}{surd}(AD/Uc ), where A is the reaction rate and Uc is the activation threshold. Perturbing apoptotic sensitivity confirmed the predicted threshold-speed relationship. These findings establish the activation threshold as a key determinant of trigger wave speed and provide a broadly applicable scaling law for predicting the spread of switch-like biochemical signals.

papers.title: Are carbohydrate ring distortions determined by biology or crystallography? The impact of experimental conditions on structural data
papers.abstract: Carbohydrates are essential molecules involved in a wide range of biological processes. While their structural representation in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) has been hindered due to their highly diverse and flexible nature, advancements on X-ray crystallography and CryoEM are accelerating the obtaining of their experimental structures, which in turn supports improved analyses of their structural properties, such as the role of their non-chair conformations on biological processes. In this context, the current work provides a comprehensive and up to date overview of carbohydrate structures within the PDB through classification, quantification, and characterization of monosaccharides and glycan chains, incorporating Cremer-Pople puckering coordinates to evaluate pyranose conformations. Our findings show that, even with a steep increase in CryoEM structures including more complex oligosaccharides, carbohydrate data remains concentrate dinsmallglycanchains, with a about 4% of non-chair conformation sintopresolution structures. Free energy landscapes for the pyranose ring in the presence and absence of nine different binding proteins, including both enzymes and non-enzymes, reinforce the preferred stability of chairs and the rarity of conformational induction upon binding.

papers.title: Danuglipron and orforglipron engage GLP-1R through materially different interfaces: an unbiased molecular dynamics study
papers.abstract: GLP-1R is among the most heavily pursued targets in metabolic disease, but its natural agonist is a 30-residue peptide that must be injected. Two oral non-peptide agonists have reached late-stage trials. Cryo-EM studies have already shown that danuglipron and CHU-128, a close analogue of orforglipron, occupy the receptor differently, but not how either interface behaves over time. We ran 500 ns of unbiased all-atom molecular dynamics on GLP-1R bound to GLP-1, danuglipron (PF-06882961) and orforglipron (LY3502970), one trajectory each, in a POPC bilayer with the G protein removed. Although CHU-128 has been simulated before, its analogue, orforglipron, has not. Scored against contacts computed from the deposited structures, under a force field that shares no parameters with previous oral agonist studies, we recovered 80%, 86% and 79% above 50% occupancy. Indexing contact by chemical group, rather than by receptor residue, and normalising by molecular size, separates the two oral compounds: orforglipron carries ring systems dedicated almost entirely to one receptor domain, one of them directing 99.7% of its contact to the extracellular domain, whereas every group of danuglipron engages both. Danuglipron is correspondingly the outlier on measures that do not depend on a chosen threshold: only 33% of its contacts exceed 90% occupancy against 72% and 84%, and it is the only system whose occupancies remain unconverged at 100 ns. With single trajectories, these are observations rather than tested claims, but two drugs of the same class and comparable size occupy this receptor in structurally distinct ways.

papers.title: 4D confocal microscopy of time dependent cell and nuclear osmotic response reveals differential osmoregulation and transport kinetics
papers.abstract: A cell's ability to maintain its volume is a prerequisite for its essential physiological functions. Changes in extracellular osmolarity induce the flux of water and solutes across the cell and nuclear membrane and, therefore, alters cell and nuclear volumes. Here, we investigated the equilibrium and dynamic volumetric responses of cells and nuclei in adherent human hepatoma (HepG2) cell monolayers using live three-dimensional imaging. Through image segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and volume rendering, precise cell and nuclear volumes were quantified. We found that during hypoosmotic stress, cells swell and lose osmolytes through active volume regulation, and nuclei undergo greater relative expansion than cells. During hyperosmotic stress, we found that both cells and nuclei shrink rapidly, develop irregular morphologies and undergo passive volume regulation. Furthermore, we explored the osmotic responses in these cells by restoring isosmotic conditions following osmotic stress and found that nuclei returned to volumes greater than their initial isosmotic volume, whereas cytoplasmic volume returned to a value below its initial isosmotic volume following swelling. By fitting coupled transport models water and solute permeability estimates for both cells and nuclei were made from their dynamic responses to different anisosmotic media with and without the presence of permeating solutes dimethyl sulfoxide and ethylene glycol. Together, these quantitative measurements of cell, cytoplasm, and nuclear volumetric responses and associated transport parameters have important implications for understanding cell physiology and the mechanism of osmoregulation.

papers.title: Mechanophenotype of synovial fibroblasts correlates with patients' pathotypes and treatment response in Rheumatoid Arthritis
papers.abstract: The mechanical features of synovial fibroblasts may encode clinically relevant information for the management of rheumatoid arthritis. Indeed, it remains poorly understood the links between cellular and microenvironment mechanics with patient stratification and therapeutic response. Here we show that combining organotypic synovial cultures with multimodal mechanophenotyping and transcriptomics identifies distinct ''soft'' and ''stiff'' fibroblast states. Healthy and rheumatoid arthritis fibroblasts were cultured in two or three dimensions (organotypic cell cultures), alone or with endothelial cells, and characterized by high-throughput nanoindentation, picobalance measurements, digital holographic microscopy, Brillouin microscopy and RNA sequencing. Three-dimensional culture reduced single-cell Young's modulus and total mass while increasing dry-mass surface density; endothelial co-culture increased fibroblast stiffness and the longitudinal modulus of intact organotypic cultures. Stiffness-based grouping revealed transcriptional programmes related to extracellular-matrix remodelling, cytoskeletal contractility, and TGF-beta, WNT, and Hippo signalling. Mapping these signatures to publicly available rheumatoid arthritis clinical transcriptomic datasets associated the ''stiff'' state with fibrotic and myeloid-fibrotic pathotypes and treatment-refractory programmes, whereas the ''soft'' state aligned with lymphoid pathotypes and rituximab- or tocilizumab-responsive programmes. These findings support mechanophenotype-associated transcriptional signatures as potential biomarkers for rheumatoid arthritis stratification.

papers.title: bioRheoFlow A Rheometric Platform for In Situ Biofilm Mechanics Under Controlled Flow Conditions
papers.abstract: Biofilm mechanics depend strongly on growth history, hydration, nutrient availability, and interfacial attachment, yet conventional rheology requires harvesting and transfer that can perturb the as-grown structure. Here, we introduce bioRheoFlow, a 3D-printed rheometer-mounted platform for cultivation and mechanical characterization without sample transfer. The platform combines evaporation compensation with static or axial nutrient flow, and benchmark measurements validate its rheometric performance. Applied to Pseudomonas putida and Pantoea sp., bioRheoFlow reveals that biofilms cultivated in situ under axial flow exhibit substantially higher elastic moduli than conventionally grown and scraped samples. Despite similar linear-viscoelastic stress ranges, the species show distinct nonlinear responses: P. putida exhibits a lower crossover stress and more abrupt failure, whereas Pantoea sp. sustains larger stresses and deformations. Creep suggests contributions from bulk deformation and biofilm-substrate interactions. bioRheoFlow provides a controlled framework for probing growth-conditioned mechanics in living biofilms.

papers.title: Electrode-Tethered DNA: Interfacial Mechanics and Switching Dynamics from Ensemble-Level Atomistic Simulations
papers.abstract: Surface-tethered DNA, anchored to gold by the late 1990s, has matured into a versatile platform for biosensing, computing and actuation. Whereas the molecular behavior of DNA in bulk solution is well characterized, that of DNA at electrode interfaces remains far less understood. Here we investigate the mechanics and dynamics of electrode-tethered double-stranded DNA across surface chemistries, salt concentrations and applied potentials. Using GPU-accelerated all-atom molecular dynamics, we sample trajectory ensembles totaling 144 s over 620 simulations. The simulations reproduce key experimental observations yet uncover molecular behavior that had gone unnoticed despite nearly three decades of research. Ensemble statistics reveal a preferred orientation about the helical axis upon surface contact. Energetic analysis identifies a substantial role for Onsager-Samaras-type repulsion in opposing that contact. By reproducing experimental trends while resolving their molecular origins, these ensembles substantially narrow the longstanding simulation-experiment gap and provide a basis for engineering tethered-DNA devices.

papers.title: Mechanical regulation of endocytosis by protein droplet capillary forces
papers.abstract: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) is the primary pathway for internalization of extracellular and membrane cargo in eukaryotic cells. It is characterized by a patch of the plasma membrane invaginating and pinching off to generate a cytoplasmic vesicle. Recently, experimental evidence has begun to accumulate in support of proteins assembling into liquid-like condensates at nascent CME sites, but potential functional consequences are not understood. Given that condensate capillary forces can influence membrane bending, we constructed complementary analytical and numerical model systems to probe the mechanical influence of a protein droplet on endocytosis. Model evaluations and analysis reveal that a droplet can regulate the progression of endocytosis by stalling invagination until the droplet grows past a threshold size. After the droplet-mediated brake is released, the droplet provides a force that can drive the membrane bud toward scission. Thus, we propose a ``mechanical timer'' mechanism as a function for protein phase separation in cellular membrane trafficking.

papers.title: e^-2 Threshold for Bistability in Non-equilibrium Sorting of Biomolecular Condensates
papers.abstract: Cells use ATP-driven chaperones to extract clients from biomolecular condensates selectively, yet no closed-form criterion links molecular parameters to condensate quality control. We derive a minimal non-equilibrium sorting reactor model that reduces the reaction-diffusion dynamics to one algebraic equation. In the idealized low-load limit, a concentration-dependent partition coefficient produces a saddle-node bifurcation between functional clearance and pathological storage. The critical Damk"ohler number is (mathrm{Da}_{0c}=e^{-2}) and is independent of the feedback strength. Corrections shift the value but preserve the topology. The model predicts a Kramers-type functional lifetime and recovery costs that scale as (R^3). Critical slowing down near the bifurcation provides early-warning signatures for FCS and FRAP.

papers.title: Methylglyoxal-derived glycation tunes nuclear viscoelasticity
papers.abstract: Reactive carbonyl metabolites such as methylglyoxal (MGO) accumulate in diabetes, aging, and metabolic disease, conditions frequently associated with pathological stiffening of human cells and tissues. While glycation of extracellular matrices and cytoskeletal proteins is known to contribute to these mechanical changes, whether the nucleus itself is a direct mechanical target of carbonyl stress remains unknown. Here, by combining advanced atomic force microscopy-based nanomechanical probing with correlative confocal imaging, we show that MGO-derived glycation directly remodels isolated cell nuclei, increasing stiffness, reducing fluidity, and restricting intranuclear deformation propagation. MGO-derived adducts accumulate prominently at the nuclear envelope, and perturbation of lamin A/C and chromatin state reveals that both structures contribute to glycation-induced stiffening. In cells, chronic MGO exposure induces nucleus-intrinsic stiffening and biases YAP nuclear localization in a substrate-stiffness-dependent manner, linking nuclear glycation to altered mechanosensitive regulation. In vivo, cardiac nuclear stiffening is only observed along with increased immunodetected MGO-adduct burden, while nuclear fluidity remains largely preserved. Together, these findings establish nonenzymatic glycation as a metabolic mechanism that remodels nuclear mechanics and alters cellular mechanosensing, revealing a previously unrecognized physical consequence of carbonyl stress.

papers.title: Distinct Aβ40 and Aβ42 co-assembly pathways with free lipids: Experiment-driven MD study
papers.abstract: Amyloid {beta}-protein (A{beta}), which is known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD), is also involved in several physiological functions. Of the two predominant isoforms, A{beta}40 and A{beta}42, the latter is more aggregation-prone and more active in health and disease. In the brain, A{beta} interacts with free lipids, which may affect its assembly pathways. Here, thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence spectroscopy is combined with molecular dynamics (MD) to investigate A{beta}40 and A{beta}42 co-assembly with free dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine (DMPC) and DMPC/cholesterol (CHOL) lipids. ThT measurements at several protein-to-lipid (PL) ratios show isoform- and lipid composition-dependent kinetics of A{beta} fibril formation with clear isoform-dependent lipid effects at a PL ratio of 1:5. Early co-assembly stages of six A{beta}40/A{beta}42 with DMPC and DMPC/CHOL lipids at this PL ratio are then examined by MD. MD results indicate that lipids alter the secondary structure more and interact more avidly with A{beta}40 than with A{beta}42. In turn, A{beta}40 increases the planar order of lipid bicelles more than A{beta}42. Unlike A{beta}40, A{beta}42 decreases the nematic order of CHOL. In DMPC/CHOL lipids, A{beta}42 but not A{beta}40 exhibits two A{beta}-lipid interaction modes associated with mutually exclusive A{beta}42-lipid and A{beta}42-A{beta}42 interactions. Our MD findings provide a plausible explanation for an experimentally observed increase in the lag time for A{beta}40 fibril formation in DMPC lipids and even more so in DMPC/CHOL lipids that contrasts with much smaller effects of lipids on A{beta}42 fibril formation and offer additional atomistic-level insights into A{beta} co-assembly with lipids amenable to experimental testing.

papers.title: Dendritic Morphology Constrains Microtubule Dynamics and Organization
papers.abstract: Neuronal dendrites form highly branched morphologies supported by spatially patterned microtubule arrays that are essential for intracellular transport and structural stability, yet how this organization is established and maintained remains unclear. Here we analyze microtubule behavior in Drosophila sensory neurons using live-cell imaging, deep learning-based analysis, and genetic perturbations. We find that microtubules are shorter and fewer in thin distal branches and progressively longer and more abundant in thicker proximal branches. Locally, polymerization slows in narrow branches due to soluble tubulin depletion, while catastrophe frequency increases near branch points upon cortical encounter. A physical model incorporating these morphology-dependent constraints reproduces both local microtubule dynamics and global organization. Inverting the textbook view that microtubule dynamics shape cell morphology, our results demonstrate that, on short timescales, cell morphology instead constrains microtubule dynamics, thereby determining large-scale cytoskeletal organization.

papers.title: Curvature sensing and generation by diverse membrane-tethered polymers can be explained by a unifying physical model
papers.abstract: Cell membranes are decorated by dense, polymeric macromolecules such as proteins with bulky intrinsically disordered regions, glycosylated proteins, and glycopolymers. Experiments have illustrated that the curvature of cellular membranes, which plays a role in diverse biological processes, can be regulated by the local density of these membrane-tethered polymers and their response to environmental changes. However, the mechanisms underlying the feedback between solution conditions, membrane curvature, and the local density and molecular weight of membrane-tethered polymers remain largely unexplored. In this work, using a combination of theory and experiment, we show that the ionic strength of the surrounding solution and the degree of ionization both play important roles in regulating the conformation of the membrane-tethered polymers, which in turn influences their membrane curvature generation capabilities. Specifically, we show that for negatively charged, disordered proteins and glycans, the thickness of the polymer brush decreases with ionic strength but increases with grafting density and degree of ionization, resulting in enhanced sensitivity to membrane curvature and an amplified ability to drive membrane curvature at lower ionic concentrations. Our findings reveal a mechanism by which membrane-tethered polymers generate membrane curvature to minimize free energy, with the extent of curvature generation modulated by the polymer grafting density and layer thickness, as well as by the ionic strength of the surrounding solution. The implications of these findings are broad, suggesting that perturbations to biopolymer charge, such as sialylation of glycans and phosphorylation of disordered proteins, could actively modulate membrane curvature induction in diverse cellular processes from endocytosis to cell motility.

papers.title: Measuring protein conformational changes with genetically encoded bipyridylalanine and transition-metal ion FRET
papers.abstract: Transition-metal ion Forster resonance energy transfer (tmFRET) measures short-range distances and conformational changes in proteins, but its distance sensitivity depends on the donor-acceptor pair. Here, we establish the metal-chelating noncanonical amino acid bipyridylalanine (bpyA) as a flexible, genetically encoded acceptor platform whose Forster distance (R0) can be tuned without changing protein labeling. Cu2+, Cu2+ complexed with nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA), and Fe2+ form distinct acceptors at the same bpyA site, allowing distance sensitivity to be adjusted by changing the solution conditions. We incorporated bpyA at two sites in maltose binding protein (MBP) and labeled nearby engineered cysteines with the donor fluorophore BODIPY. The resulting [Cu(bpyA)]2+, [CuNTA(bpyA)]2+, and [Fe(bpyA)]2+ acceptors provided R0 values ranging from 13.9 to 21.2 [A]. Analysis of time-resolved tmFRET data recovered donor-acceptor distance distributions and maltose-dependent changes consistent with structural predictions. At the 237/295 site pair, both copper and iron acceptors resolved the maltose-dependent decrease in distance. At the 309/322 site pair, [Cu(bpyA)]2+ did not appreciably resolve the distance increase, whereas adding NTA shifted R0 toward shorter distances and enabled detection of an increase from 12.1 to 14.4 [A]. These results demonstrate that a single bpyA-labeled protein preparation supports multiple tmFRET acceptors, providing a cysteine-independent acceptor-labeling strategy with adjustable distance sensitivity.
